content: The O'nyong'nyong virus was first identified in 1959 by the Uganda Virus Research Institute located in Entebbe, Uganda. It belongs to the Togaviridae family and is classified under the Alphavirus genus. This virus is closely related to the Chikungunya virus and the Igbo Ora virus. The name O'nyong'nyong originates from the Nilotic languages spoken in Uganda and Sudan, and it translates to weakening of the joints. The virus is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected mosquito. Notably, it is the only known virus primarily spread by anopheline mosquitoes, specifically Anopheles funestus and Anopheles gambiae. Individuals infected with the O'nyong'nyong virus typically present with symptoms such as polyarthritis, a rash, and fever. Additional symptoms may include pain in the eyes, chest pain, inflammation of the lymph nodes (lymphadenitis), and a general sense of lethargy. Importantly, no fatalities have been reported as a result of infection with this virus. There have been two documented epidemics of O'nyong'nyong fever. The first epidemic occurred between 1959 and 1962, beginning in Uganda and subsequently spreading to Kenya, Tanzania, Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), Malawi, and Mozambique. This outbreak affected over two million individuals, making it one of the largest recorded epidemics caused by an arbovirus. During this outbreak, the virus was first isolated from mosquito specimens and human blood samples collected in Gulu, a region in northern Uganda, in 1959. The second epidemic took place between 1996 and 1997 and was limited to Uganda, affecting approximately 400 individuals. The 35-year gap between these two outbreaks, along with historical evidence of a similar outbreak in Uganda between 1904 and 1906, suggests that epidemics of the O'nyong'nyong virus may follow a cyclical pattern, occurring every 30 to 50 years.
